title: Tries
relevance: Tries are a common SDE interview and OA topic for prefix search, word dictionaries, and XOR-based bitwise optimization.

phases.goal: Establish what a trie is and why prefix operations run in time proportional to word length.

must_hit.point: A trie is an n-ary tree where each edge is a character and each root-to-node path spells a string prefix.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes edges as characters and paths as prefixes, not as storing full strings at each node.

must_hit.point: A boolean flag at a node marks the end of a valid word.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions isEnd (or equivalent) so prefixes and complete words can be distinguished.

must_hit.point: Insertion, search, and prefix-matching take O(L) time, where L is the word length, independent of how many words are stored.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States O(L) and that cost does not grow with the number of stored words.

must_hit.point: For lowercase English, a canonical node uses a fixed-size child array of size 26.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions next[26] or equivalent fixed alphabet indexing via ch - 'a'.

probes: What is a trie, and why are insert/search/prefix checks O(L) regardless of how many words are in it?

hints.1: Think about how words share paths for common prefixes.
hints.2: Each step follows one character edge; you walk at most L edges.
hints.3: n-ary tree, edge = character, path = prefix; end-of-word flag; time O(L) independent of dictionary size.

phases.goal: Show how insert, search, startsWith, and counter-augmented frequency/erase operations walk the trie.

must_hit.point: On insert, walk each character from the root, creating a missing child when needed, then set isEnd on the final node.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes create-if-absent per character and marking the last node as a word end.

must_hit.point: search requires reaching the final node with isEnd true; startsWith only requires that the prefix path exists.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly separates path existence from the end-of-word flag.

must_hit.point: For frequency queries, augment nodes with cntEnd (words ending here) and cntPrefix (words sharing this path); insert increments them, erase decrements them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both counters and says insert increments along the path / at end, erase decrements the same counters.

must_hit.point: Basic insert is O(L) time and O(L) space; search and startsWith are O(L) time with O(1) auxiliary space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls O(L) for all three and O(1) extra space for the queries.

probes: Walk through insert, search, and startsWith on the same word—what differs at the last node?

hints.1: Both search and startsWith follow the same character path.
hints.2: Ask what happens if the path exists but isEnd is false.
hints.3: search returns final isEnd; startsWith returns true once the prefix path is fully walked.

phases.goal: Compare child maps, memory layout, and when a trie beats a hash set.

must_hit.point: For small alphabets, a fixed child array beats unordered_map because lookups are cache-friendly with zero-overhead O(1) access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers array of 26 for lowercase English and cites cache-friendly O(1) lookups.

must_hit.point: For large alphabets such as full Unicode, array memory is prohibitive, so hash maps or balanced BSTs are used instead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Switches to map/BST when the alphabet is huge.

must_hit.point: A hash set gives O(1) exact-word lookup, but a trie unlocks prefix queries and ordered traversals.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts exact membership with prefix/autocomplete capability.

must_hit.point: To avoid pointer allocations, an index-pool vector of array<int, 26> can represent children as integer indices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions vector<array<int, 26>> (or equivalent) instead of Node*.

probes: When would you store children in an unordered_map instead of next[26], and when is a trie preferable to a hash set?

hints.1: Consider alphabet size and what queries you need.
hints.2: Small fixed alphabet favors arrays; Unicode favors maps; exact lookup vs prefixes.
hints.3: Array of 26 for English; map/BST for Unicode; hash set for exact words, trie for prefixes and ordered walks.

phases.goal: Apply tries to prefix dictionary problems, distinct substrings, and binary XOR tries.

must_hit.point: For longest word with all prefixes present, insert all words then require isEnd true on every node along the word's path (or DFS only along isEnd edges).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Checks every proper prefix is also a stored word via isEnd along the path.

must_hit.point: Distinct substrings: insert every suffix into one trie; each unique root-to-node path is one distinct substring, equal to the node count excluding the root.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains suffixes in a trie and counting non-root nodes as distinct substrings.

must_hit.point: A binary XOR trie uses next[2] and inserts 32-bit numbers MSB-first; max XOR greedily prefers the opposite bit at each level.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions bit trie, 32 bits from MSB, and taking the opposite branch when present.

must_hit.point: For max XOR under an upper bound m_i, sort queries by m_i offline and insert nums in ascending order so each element is inserted once before needed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes offline sort by limit and sweeping insertions into one trie.

probes: How would you find the maximum XOR of two numbers in an array using a trie, and how does the offline-sort trick help when each query also has an upper bound m?

hints.1: Store numbers as bit paths and try to mismatch bits.
hints.2: Insert 32 bits MSB→LSB; query greedily takes the opposite bit; for bounds, sort by m and insert gradually.
hints.3: Binary trie next[2]; greedy opposite bit adds that bit to XOR; sort queries by m_i and nums ascending, insert nums ≤ m before each query.

tradeoffs.topic: Fixed array of 26 vs unordered_map for children
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Small alphabets (lowercase English) favor next[26] for cache-friendly zero-overhead O(1) child lookup; large alphabets like full Unicode make the array too memory-heavy, so use a hash map or balanced BST.

tradeoffs.topic: Hash set vs trie for a word dictionary
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A hash set gives O(1) exact-word lookup, but a trie supports prefix queries (startsWith/autocomplete) and ordered traversals that a flat set does not.

tradeoffs.topic: Heap Node* pointers vs index-pool vector<array<int, 26>>
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Pointer nodes are simple but allocation-heavy; an index-pool stores children as integer indices in a vector of fixed arrays to avoid dynamic Node allocations when memory or GC is a bottleneck.

gotchas.trap: Treating path existence as proof that a full word was inserted.
gotchas.correction: search must check the final node's isEnd; startsWith only needs the prefix path to exist.

gotchas.trap: Underestimating trie memory cost or defaulting to maps for English letters.
gotchas.correction: Each node holds 26 child pointers (many null), so tries are memory-heavy; for small alphabets prefer fixed arrays, and consider an index-pool if allocations hurt.

gotchas.trap: Building a fresh XOR trie per query when answers are constrained by m_i.
gotchas.correction: Sort queries by m_i and nums ascending, then insert each num once when it becomes eligible—offline sweeping, not rebuild-per-query.

gotchas.trap: Counting distinct substrings by inserting the string once or counting only leaves.
gotchas.correction: Insert every suffix; each unique path (non-root node) is one distinct substring because identical prefixes merge in the trie.
